statement: Triangle $T$ has side lengths $3$, $4$ and $5$. Consider all points, inside or outside $T$, whose distance to the nearest point on a side of $T$ is at most $1$. What is the area of the region made up of these points?

choices.misconception: I counted only the part of the region outside the triangle and forgot the points inside it.
I counted the triangle and the three strips along the sides, but left out the rounded pieces at the three corners.
I put a half circle of radius $1$ at each corner, instead of pieces that fit together into one full circle.
I put a full circle of radius $1$ at each corner, instead of pieces that fit together into one full circle.

hints: Split the region into the part outside $T$ and the part inside $T$.

Outside: a strip of width $1$ along each side, plus rounded pieces at the corners. The corner pieces are sectors of radius $1$ whose angles are the exterior angles of $T$. Inside: which points of $T$ are more than $1$ away from every side?

The exterior angles add to $360^\circ$, so the corner pieces make one full circle. The inscribed circle of a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle has radius $1$, so no point inside is more than $1$ from the sides. The total is $6 + (3 + 4 + 5) \cdot 1 + \pi$.

solutions.reliable: Outside $T$, the region is a $1 \times 3$, a $1 \times 4$ and a $1 \times 5$ rectangle along the sides, total area $12$, together with a sector of radius $1$ at each corner. The angle of each sector is $180^\circ$ minus the triangle's angle there, and these add to $3 \cdot 180^\circ - 180^\circ = 360^\circ$, so the three sectors make one circle of area $\pi$. Inside $T$, the point farthest from all three sides is the center of the inscribed circle, and its distance to the sides is the inradius $r$. From area $= r \cdot \frac{\text{perimeter}}{2}$ we get $6 = r \cdot 6$, so $r = 1$. So every point of $T$ is within $1$ of a side, and all of $T$, area $6$, is in the region. The total area is $12 + \pi + 6 = 18 + \pi$.
